newsitem.title: FRANCE: German President meets French Jewish leaders.
newsitem.headline: German President meets French Jewish leaders.

text.p: German President Roman Herzog and French Jewish leaders delved into past and future on Friday, puzzling over why one of the world's most cultured nations spawned the Nazis and seeking ways to prevent any repeat.

"How could the people of Goethe, Schiller and Beethoven have given themselves such infamous leaders? Why, with the exception of a handful of heroes, did the Germans participate in murder with such intensity?" Jewish leader Jean Kahn asked Herzog.

The German president, on a four-day visit to France, agreed "it is truly incomprehensible that an entire people to whom all had been announced in advance (by the Nazis) followed such a government in the execution of such a programme.
"Perhaps, for some, it was a bit because what was promised (the extermination of European Jewry) seemed so incredible they did not believe it would happen.
"Perhaps for others, it was the fruit of their own misery between the wars that blinded them to the misery others would suffer," said Herzog.

The dialogue, lasting over two hours and concluded with a visit to Paris' Great Synagogue, was at Herzog's request and aimed at symbolising German remorse for the persecution of Jews in France during the World War Two occupation.
Some 76,000 Jews, including 11,000 children, were deported from France to Nazi death camps. There are now about 750,000 Jews in France, Western Europe's largest Jewish community.

Herzog, whose office is largely ceremonial, was flanked during the meeting by aides and civil rights campaigners from former East Germany who he invited to join him on his trip, the first state visit to France by a German president since 1984.

Kahn, president of the "Consistoire Israelite de France," a body created by Napoleon to head Jewish religious affairs, paid lavish personal tribute to Herzog for siding with Jews in a spat with then-Polish President Lech Walesa at the site of the former Auschwitz death camp in January 1995.

The Jews, led by Kahn, had held a separate memorial service, which Herzog attended, after Walesa made a speech marking the 50th anniversary of the liberation of the camp but omitting to mention that 90 percent who those killed there were Jews.

Auschwitz survivor Henri Bulawko told Herzog he believed Germany had not fully come to terms with its past and cited state pensions to families of executed war criminals and members of S.S. units which ran death camps.
Herzog recalled he had instituted a day of remembrance for victims of the Nazis and sought to instruct German youth about their country's troubled past.

"Every year we will hold ceremonies. But let me be frank, what really counts is that the subject be debated in schools, newspapers and associations so that our population can reflect on the crimes committed.

"Generations are changing and speak a different language. What now counts is to properly transmit the knowledge of what happened so that it is made real and is not just a dry history lesson," he said.
